La liberté de Soolking, le rappeur algér: Soolking’s Liberté: The Algerian Rapper Who Brings Generations Together
Soolking est l’un des premiers artistes: Soolking is one of the first artists in France to have brought Maghrebi sounds into rap.
Les apprentis journalistes de l'École Co: The apprentice journalists of École Converse meet Franco-Algerian rapper Soolking.
Fatima Bah, Marc-Elder Piard, Naila Naou: Fatima Bah, Marc-Elder Piard, Naila Naoui and Ahmed El Moudden, apprentice journalists at École Converse, meet Franco-Algerian rapper Soolking.
Le 5 mai dernier, le rappeur franco-algé: On May 5, Franco-Algerian rapper Soolking, one of the most prominent francophone artists of his generation, performed at the Olympia de Montréal. With his rhythms of raï, reggae and R&B, the artist is reaching a growing young audience. From Algiers to Montréal, the influence of Soolking, whose real name is Abderraouf Derradji, crosses borders. Five hours before the concert, young Maghrebi teenagers wait in line, hoping to meet their idol. But what would they want to ask Soolking? “What’s the secret to success? How did you get where you are? Who pushed you to start?”
<strong>‍</strong>Soolking compte deux a: ‍Soolking has two albums to his name, and a highly anticipated third will be released on May 27. Dressed in an Akatsuki outfit from the manga Naruto, the artist tells us he is currently working on publishing a manga, a kind of Japanese comic book from which he took his rapper name. Abderraouf Derradji, who is 32, has lived in France since 2014. The rapper does not hesitate to bring his cultural background into his art, a mark of authenticity that his audience responds to. “Many young people today […] who come from the home country and go to Europe, the United States, Canada, bring their musical heritage with them. It lets them stand out from the others right away,” he says. Soolking is one of the first artists in France to have brought Maghrebi sounds into rap.
<strong><em>‍</em></strong>Si Soolking a: ‍While Soolking likes to sing about success and love, he sometimes feels the need to tackle more political themes. That is what comes through when listening to the emblematic song Guérilla and, more recently, the song Liberté.
Cette pièce est issue d’une collaboratio: The track is the result of a collaboration with <l1>the anonymous singers’ group Ouled El Bahdja</l1>. Politically engaged, Ouled El Bahdja has come to embody the desire for change in Algeria. When the group performs on national television, the sound is sometimes cut so the audience cannot hear the lyrics. Its members never give interviews.
Dans sa loge avant son concert, Soolking: In his dressing room before the concert, Soolking tells us how Liberté came to be.
« J’écoutais un morceau qu’ils avaient f: “I was listening to a track they had made, called Ultima Verba, and as luck would have it, in the chorus they say ‘freedom.’ So I thought: honestly, I have to invite them, take their chorus, and that way, in the verses, I can say what I’ve wanted to say from the start,” the artist explains.
Sortie en mars 2019,<em> Liberté</em> ex: Released in March 2019, Liberté expresses the hopes of several generations for a better future in Algeria, where the song was a phenomenal success. From Montréal to Paris and all across Algeria, it was quickly embraced by the Algerian people and their diaspora as the anthem of the Hirak protests. For more than three years, Algerians demonstrated against the regime in power, pushing President Abdelaziz Bouteflika to resign after 20 years in office and demanding a change of system. It is in this context that Soolking’s songs transcended generations. His concerts are not only full of young people. Their parents are there too, just as receptive as their children to the rapper’s denunciations and political hopes.
Lorsqu’on aborde la question avec lui, A: When we raise the subject with him, Abderraouf Derradji admits he wasn’t thinking of the Hirak in particular. “I wasn’t necessarily aiming at one situation, one moment or one thing. It just happened, like they say, the stars aligned. There were protests in Algeria, there were protests in Lebanon, there was the re-election in Tunisia, and this and that. There were the yellow vests. So at that point, since it came out then, it had a big impact because a lot of people made it their own in relation to what was happening in their countries.” He goes on to add that others embraced the track because of their thirst for freedom. “There are other people who adopted it because, already in their everyday lives [...] they needed freedom, a message of freedom,” suggests the performer.
<strong>‍</strong>Malgré ce qu’elle fait: ‍Despite what it promises, fame is sometimes hard to live with for the international rapper, who fears losing his humanity. What does he suggest to young people who want to follow in his footsteps? Keep their feet on the ground and, above all, start a project for the right reasons. “The famous side is the bad side of this job,” he confides. “You become like a marketing product, like a T-shirt. A T-shirt, you’re walking down the street, you can say to it: ‘I like it, but I don’t really like the stitching.’ You can shake it. But you, you become like a T-shirt. And there are some people, not all, thankfully, who forget you’re a human being. So you have to go easy on the buzz,” he adds in the same breath.
Si la gloire est au rendez-vous, le chem: While glory has arrived, the path has nonetheless been strewn with obstacles for the musician. Today’s international star was yesterday a homeless person without immigration status. The rapper went to France without status to pursue a career in the music world. And there were times when he found himself with nowhere to sleep. Before becoming <l1>Soolking, Abderraouf slept on the streets of France.</l1>
<l1>‍</l1>Les obstacles ont été formateu: <l1>‍</l1>The obstacles were formative, according to the rapper. “Failure, I think, is more important than success in a career. Because failure makes you question yourself [...] It makes you learn,” he explains with complete humility. The love his fans have for him moves him enormously. That is why he is always ready to offer them advice so they can reach their goals. “Young people who want to get started in any field, medicine, music, sports, studies, whatever, I tell them you have to be determined, you have to believe in it, not give up, and also give yourself the means. It’s not: ‘We sleep at home and tell ourselves: well, me, I’m unlucky anyway.’ No, you have to get up. You have to go for it, try, attempt, push, really. And if it doesn’t work, at least, in your own self-esteem, you’ll say: ‘I tried anyway.’”
C’est avec ces messages, qu’on retrouve: It is through these messages, found in the lyrics of his songs and throughout our meeting, that we understand why Soolking inspires young people wherever he goes.
